title: What this system actually is, end to end, and which parts can fail independently
content:
Five moving parts, and knowing which one owns a symptom is most of the diagnosis.

Supabase Postgres is the system of record and also, unusually, most of the business logic: routines in schema public do the work that in other systems would sit in an application tier. Supabase Edge Functions are Deno workers deployed alongside it and are the only network-facing entry to the database for the portals; they hold no long-lived process and no local state. Next.js on Vercel serves the website and the customer and supplier portals and also owns the schedule -- see the scheduler records, because that is the least obvious part of this topology. Resend delivers email. Stripe takes payment through hosted Checkout. Twilio carries WhatsApp and SMS.

What can fail independently, which is the useful cut. The database can be healthy while every edge function is failing, because deploys are per function. Edge functions can be healthy while the schedule is dead, because the schedule lives outside them. The website can serve perfectly while every write fails, because reads are cached and writes are not. Email can be accepted by Resend and never reach an inbox, because acceptance and delivery are different events. Payment can succeed at Stripe and never be recorded here, because the record is written by a webhook that can fail on its own.

That last pattern generalises and is worth carrying: at every boundary between two of these five, there are two separate facts -- the thing happened over there, and we know it happened over here -- and an outage is usually the second one, not the first. When somebody reports that something did not happen, the first question is whether it did not happen or whether we merely did not record it.

parts.database: Supabase Postgres, system of record and most business logic
parts.compute: Supabase Edge Functions, Deno, stateless, per-function deploys
parts.web: Next.js on Vercel, website plus customer and supplier portals, and the scheduler

independent_failures: database healthy, edge functions failing (per-function deploys)
edge functions healthy, schedule dead (the schedule is outside them)
structured_data.generalisation: at every boundary there are two facts -- it happened, and we know it happened -- and the outage is usually the second

title: There is exactly one Supabase project, and a check that reads the deleted one returns a green light over nothing
content:
There is ONE Supabase project and its reference is htdblwldjkcgjvmqkbeh. Everything -- production data, every edge function, every routine -- lives there.

A second project existed as staging and was DELETED in August 2026 at the founder's instruction, for two stated reasons: he did not want old references from a stale copy feeding back into the build, and he did not want a second project costing money. It is not to be recreated, not to be deployed to, and not to be read.

The operational consequence that matters for a monitoring seat, and it is the reason this is a record rather than a footnote. A check that queries the deleted project does not fail loudly. The request four-hundred-and-four-s, and a comparison that finds no differences between here and a project that returned nothing reports NO DRIFT. That is a green light over an absence -- the exact shape of a guard that cannot fire, and it looked like a passing parity check for as long as nobody read what it was comparing against.

So: if you find a check, a script or a monitor that names a second project reference, it is not a safety net, it is a false positive generator, and the finding is the check rather than the drift. The replacement discipline is that production proves itself -- read the definition back out of the one database and compare it to the file, rather than comparing one database to another.

The same logic applies to any comparison against something that might not exist. Before trusting a difference of zero, prove that both sides were actually read.

title: pg_cron is dead: the scheduler moved out of the database entirely
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026, and this is the single most load-bearing fact about the current estate.

The cron.job table holds one row and it is inactive. Zero active jobs. The one surviving definition is an old WhatsApp flush on a two-minute schedule, switched off. The most recent entry in cron.job_run_details started on 7 September 2026 and nothing has run since.

What happened: on 7 September 2026 the founder ordered the structure dismantled, and in that change 234 cron jobs were deleted and 110 scheduling statements were stripped out of 66 files in the repository. pg_cron is still installed; it simply has nothing to run.

THE TRAP THAT WILL CATCH ANY MONITOR WRITTEN AGAINST THE OLD SHAPE. cron.job_run_details still holds tens of thousands of rows from the last seven days, and every one of them reads succeeded. Deleting a job does not delete its history. So a monitor that counts recent runs sees a busy, entirely successful scheduler; a monitor that counts jobs sees a number; and both are describing a system that is not scheduling anything. The jobs those runs belonged to no longer exist. This is run history outliving its producer, and it is why any scheduler check must join the run history back to the current job list rather than counting rows.

Anything you find that assumes the database schedules its own work -- an alert sourcing its inputs from active cron jobs, a check counting cron reds, a routine expecting to be woken -- is reading an empty set and reporting calm. Verify against the record describing where the schedule actually lives now.

structured_data.cause: the 7 Sep 2026 dismantling: 234 jobs deleted, 110 schedule statements stripped from 66 files
structured_data.trap: run history outlives deleted jobs, so recent-run counts look busy and successful while nothing is scheduled
structured_data.correct_check: join run history to the current job list; never count run rows alone
structured_data.consequence: any alert sourcing from active cron jobs reads an empty set and reports calm

title: The live scheduler is a Vercel cron hitting resilience_ping every fifteen minutes
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026. The company's entire schedule is one entry in vercel.json: a cron on a fifteen-minute expression calling the route /api/resilience-ping. That route runs on Node, optionally checks a bearer secret, and posts an empty body to the resilience_ping edge function with a thirty-second timeout, returning a bad-gateway status if the function does not come back with an ok verdict. It holds no secrets of its own.

Why it moved: running this on GitHub Actions consumed about two thousand eight hundred and eighty Actions minutes a month, which was well over the allowance. The schedule was moved to Vercel because it was the cheaper place to hold a clock.

THE CONSEQUENCE THAT MATTERS. resilience_ping is no longer a watchdog. It is the scheduler. Everything the company does on a timer is a tick inside it, executed in order on each invocation, and it drives them itself rather than waking anything else. That means the fifteen-minute Vercel cron is a single point of failure for every timed behaviour in the business at once -- digests, rating requests, backups, weekly reports, metering and message flushing all stop together and none of them will report its own absence, because the thing that would have reported it is the thing that stopped.

So the monitor that matters is not on any individual tick. It is on the heartbeat itself: has resilience_ping been invoked within the last interval, measured from the evidence of its own effects rather than from the cron configuration. A cron entry existing in vercel.json is a claim; a row written in the last fifteen minutes is a measurement.

There is a second, independent daily invocation from a GitHub Actions workflow that curls the function directly. It exists specifically as a cross-check from outside Vercel, so that a Vercel-side scheduling failure is visible from somewhere Vercel does not control.

structured_data.route: src/app/api/resilience-ping/route.ts, Node runtime, optional CRON_SECRET bearer, thirty-second timeout, posts to the edge function
structured_data.why_moved: GitHub Actions consumed roughly 2880 Actions-minutes a month, over the allowance

title: What resilience_ping actually does on each tick, in order, and why every tick swallows its own errors
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026 by reading the function. On each invocation resilience_ping performs, in this order: the CEO end-of-day digest tick, idempotent and timezone-aware for Dubai; the support rating-request tick, which asks for a rating three weeks after a reveal; the backup tick, which checks whether a Dropbox backup is due and if so drives the backup function in bounded batches; the accountant weekly report tick, which renders through the PDF function into the agent documents bucket and then attaches the result; the OpenRouter metering tick, which reads the credits and key endpoints and feeds a reading to the accountant; and the WhatsApp tick, which counts queued notifications on the WhatsApp channel and drives the sender in bounded batches -- this last one is what replaced the deleted database-side flush job. Then it evaluates a liveness routine, and if the answer is unhealthy it dedupes for half an hour against a stored marker, raises a platform-down alert, and force-flushes the outbox.

EVERY ONE OF THOSE TICKS CATCHES ITS OWN ERRORS. That is deliberate and correct: a failure inside the backup tick must not prevent the WhatsApp tick from running, because the alternative is that one broken feature silences the clock for all of them.

But it has an exact diagnostic consequence and this is the reason the record exists. A tick can fail on every invocation, for days, and the function will still return an ok verdict, the route will still return success, and the heartbeat will still look perfect. Swallowing is right for availability and blinding for observability, and here it is only half-mitigated.

Therefore: NEVER conclude that a timed behaviour is running from the fact that resilience_ping is healthy. They are different claims. To check a tick, check the effect the tick is supposed to produce -- the digest row, the rating request, the backup artefact, the weekly report, the metering reading, the drop in queued WhatsApp messages -- and check its timestamp. Per-tick evidence is the only honest signal; the ok verdict covers the loop, not the work.

structured_data.then: liveness routine; if unhealthy, half-hour dedupe, platform-down alert, forced outbox flush
structured_data.every_tick: catches its own errors so one failure cannot stop the others
structured_data.diagnostic_consequence: a tick can fail on every invocation for days while the verdict, the route and the heartbeat all read healthy
structured_data.rule: never infer a tick ran from resilience_ping being healthy; check the effect and its timestamp

title: How code reaches production: four workflows, and the one thing no workflow does
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026 by reading the workflow files. There are four.

The function deploy workflow triggers on a push to ANY branch, filtered to paths under the functions directory, the Supabase config and the deploy script itself; it also accepts a manual dispatch taking a target project and a list of slugs. It computes which slugs changed by diffing against the previous commit and drives the deploy script. Promotion to production happens only on the main branch. A manual dispatch is therefore the way to redeploy something whose files did not change.

The parity workflow runs on pull requests, on pushes to main, on a daily schedule and on demand. It asserts that the repository and the database agree, and separately runs the check that the anonymous role cannot execute a definer routine, with paid AI explicitly disabled; that job fails hard if the check merely SKIPS, which is the right design -- a skipped security check must never read as a pass.

The general checks workflow runs the test suite, lints migrations, typechecks, and runs the Deno type check over the gated functions and then advisorily over all of them. Deno check is the green build for edge functions.

The fourth is the daily out-of-band invocation of the heartbeat described elsewhere.

THE THING NO WORKFLOW DOES: NOTHING APPLIES SQL. There is no pipeline that runs a migration. Schema and routine changes are applied out of band by a person or an agent running the apply script against the one project, which reads the definition back out of the database afterwards and matches it against the file. So when you are asked why a routine in production does not match the repository, the answer is never that a deploy failed -- there was no deploy. Either the apply was never run, or it was run and something later replaced the routine.

workflows.project-parity: pull request, push to main, daily schedule, manual; repository-database agreement plus the anon-cannot-execute-definer check with paid AI disabled; fails hard if that check SKIPs
workflows.checks: test suite, migration lint, typecheck, deno check over gated functions then advisory over all
workflows.resilience-ping: daily out-of-band invocation of the heartbeat

structured_data.consequence: a production routine differing from the repository is never a failed deploy -- either the apply never ran, or something replaced it later

title: The founder-mail gate: an unregistered kind is not dropped and not raised, it is ROUTED
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026 by reading the live routine body, because the belief in circulation was that an unregistered kind is silently dropped. IT IS NOT. This record states what the code does.

Every attempt to notify the founder passes a kind. The routine trims it, defaults an empty one to the literal unregistered, and looks that kind up in the mail policy table to see whether it is allowed to email. An unregistered kind finds NO ROW, so the allowed flag comes back null, and a null treated as false sends it down the not-allowed branch. That branch does not throw and does not discard. It calls the routing routine, writes a founder alert row with its channel set to routed and a detail line naming the owner and the task number it created, and returns a result with emailed set to false. The routing routine defaults the owner when the policy has none and opens or bumps exactly one task per condition, marking in its result whether the kind was registered at all.

There is no raise anywhere in the routine. So the failure mode is not a lost message and not an exception -- it is a message that quietly becomes a task instead of an email, and the ONLY way a caller can detect that its kind was unrecognised is to read the registered flag in the returned object. A caller that ignores the return value cannot tell the two outcomes apart.

What to do with that. When investigating why the founder did not receive something, do not conclude it vanished: look for the routed alert row and the task it opened. And when adding a new notification kind, register it in the policy table in the same change, then verify by reading the returned flag rather than by watching for an email that will never arrive either way.

The fail-open direction is deliberate and correct: the safe default is not to email him. A typo degrades to a task, never to a surprise message.

title: Credentials do NOT rotate themselves any more, and the whole estate becomes due at once in about two months
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026, and this is a finding rather than a description. The received wisdom is that internal credentials rotate themselves on a daily job ahead of expiry. That is no longer true.

What is actually there. The internal credential table holds ninety-one credentials, eighty-four of them active, sixty-two carrying an expiry, and EXACTLY ONE has ever been rotated. Expiries run from early August to early September 2027, a one-year horizon from issuance. The health view defines rotation as due when a credential is active, not legacy, older than ninety days, and either never rotated or last rotated more than ninety days ago.

What is missing. The daily rotation job was deleted in the 7 September purge -- its history shows it ran exactly twice, on two consecutive mornings, and then the job ceased to exist. There is NO rotation routine anywhere in the database: a search of routine names and bodies for rotation turns up only the built-in log rotator and two unrelated helpers. The source file that is credited with creating the rotation is not present in the repository. And the red-view alert that would have surfaced this sources its inputs from ACTIVE cron jobs, of which there are none, so it reports nothing.

THE SHAPE OF THE PROBLEM, which is why it deserves an alert rather than a note. The count of credentials currently due for rotation is zero. That zero is not health -- it is arithmetic: the oldest credential is only about thirty-seven days old, under the ninety-day rule. Around early November 2026 essentially the entire estate crosses ninety days within days of each other and becomes due simultaneously, with nothing scheduled to act on it. Authentication refuses an expired credential, so this is an outage with a date on it, not a hygiene item.

This is the lens about a zero that cannot distinguish a dead guard from a clean system, in its most concrete form available today.

title: There is no registration function: account creation happens inside the sign-in code path
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026. Searching the functions directory for a registration handler returns nothing, and that absence is the most important thing to know before investigating a registration complaint. Registration is not a feature with its own entry point; it is a side effect of verifying a sign-in code.

The account-creating path is the one-time-password sign-in function. Email is the identity throughout. On a successful verification it ensures an auth user exists, creating one with a confirmed email and a random password, then mints a session. It then touches the business tables: for a buyer it marks the customer row verified and, if no row was updated, inserts one; for a supplier it marks the claimed lead's owner verified. Along the way it reads and writes verification records for email and phone, consults the suppression list, reads secrets, writes a run record and calls the rate limiter.

A phone number cannot create an account. That path is refused explicitly with a not-found status and a message telling the caller to sign up by email, and the refusal happens BEFORE any messaging charge is incurred, which is deliberate.

The mobile one-time-password function adds and verifies a phone, and will insert a customer row keyed on email if none exists before setting the phone and its verified flag.

The customer API deliberately no longer creates accounts. It was changed in August 2026 so that a read against a missing profile returns a forbidden status with a message saying accounts are created when a buyer verifies their sign-in code, not by reading an endpoint. It separately gates request submission on profile completeness and returns a precondition-required status with an explicit list of what is missing.

So a report that registration is broken can mean four different things -- the code never arrived, verification failed, the customer row was not created, or the profile is incomplete and a later step is refusing -- and they live in three different functions. Establish which before reading any code.

title: The comparison engine: one function, one cache that has never held a row, and two report tables nothing calls
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026. The founder asks about the generated comparison report lagging, so what exists needs stating precisely.

One edge function performs the comparison. It carries a deterministic module used as a model-free fallback when every paid attempt fails, and that module has its own test. Other functions mention comparison but are callers or references, not the engine.

It reads and upserts a comparison cache keyed by inquiry, a hash of the quotes and a language. THE CACHE HOLDS ZERO ROWS. Nothing has ever been cached. The function's own log line says as much in words: that the result could not be written to the cache, so every re-open re-runs the model at full cost. That is simultaneously a cost defect and the most likely cause of a report that feels slow on second and subsequent views -- the second view is not a cache hit, it is a full recomputation.

Two further tables exist that look like report storage. One holds comparisons with a publication state and a superseding pointer; the other holds versioned runs with a deterministic result and separate explanations per language. BOTH HOLD ZERO ROWS AND NEITHER IS REFERENCED BY THE LIVE FUNCTION. They are finished capability with no entry point -- complete schemas, sensible designs, and nothing that can ever fill them. Their emptiness is not the finding; their unreachability is.

NONE OF THE THREE TABLES HAS A DURATION OR TIMING COLUMN. The function enforces an internal wall-clock budget by subtracting elapsed time from a limit and passing the remainder downstream as a client timeout, but that budget is never persisted. So the only timing evidence anywhere is the run record's start and finish timestamps, and there is no duration column even there -- it must be computed from the two.

Read the companion record on how to actually investigate a slow comparison before reaching for any of this.

title: What instrumentation actually exists, and the three places to look before anywhere else
content:
MEASURED 9 SEPTEMBER 2026. This estate has less purpose-built instrumentation than its size suggests, so knowing the real inventory saves the first twenty minutes of every investigation.

The run record table is the closest thing to an application log. It carries a start and a finish timestamp per run and NO duration column, so every latency question is a subtraction. It is written by the functions themselves at the end of their work, which has an important consequence: a function that crashed or timed out may have written NO row at all, so absence in the run record is evidence of failure rather than evidence of nothing happening. It is also dominated by a small number of high-frequency callers, so a raw count of runs is a count of heartbeats and tells you almost nothing about business activity -- it is a scheduler log, not an activity log.

The platform's own edge function logs are the second place, and they hold what the run record cannot: the requests that never got far enough to write a row, the non-two-hundred responses, and the runtime errors.

The third is the database itself. Because most business logic lives in routines, the effect of a piece of work is usually a row somewhere, and the timestamp on that row is often the most reliable latency and liveness signal available -- more reliable than any log, because it is written by the same transaction that did the work.

The order to use them in: ask the database what the last real effect was and when; then read the platform logs for the window around it; then use the run record to attribute it to a caller. Going the other way -- starting from a log search -- produces a lot of reading and few conclusions, because the logs do not know what the work was supposed to achieve.

inventory.run_record: start and finish timestamps, no duration column; written at the END of work, so a crash or timeout writes no row at all
inventory.edge_logs: the platform's own function logs -- requests that never wrote a row, non-two-hundred responses, runtime errors
inventory.database_effects: the row a piece of work produces, timestamped by the same transaction that did it

title: Secrets live in a database table, and what that means for blast radius and for logging
content:
Secrets in this estate are held in a table in the public schema rather than in a dedicated secret store. That is a deliberate arrangement that the security corpus documents in detail, and this record covers only the operational consequences a monitoring seat must act on.

First, blast radius. Anything that can read that table can read every credential in it -- provider keys, the shared secrets that let machines call edge functions, and the markers various routines store. There is no per-secret access boundary. So the question who can read this table is the same question as who holds every key, and it must be answered from the actual grants and row-security state rather than from intent.

Second, and this is the one that produces incidents rather than audit findings: a secret in a table is a value that ordinary queries return. Any diagnostic that selects broadly, any error message that includes a row, any export, any debug dump, and any log line that prints a query result is a potential disclosure. The discipline is absolute and simple -- never select the value column when you only need to know whether a key exists, never include it in an error, and never paste a row into a report or a message. Select the key name and a boolean for whether the value is present.

Third, the shared-secret convention. Machine callers authenticate to edge functions by presenting a secret drawn from that table under a naming convention. It is a bearer credential: whoever has the string is the caller. That is why the credential expiry position matters so much, and why a leaked function log is a more serious event here than in a system using short-lived tokens.

When you find a secret in a place it should not be, treat it as compromised rather than as exposed-but-probably-fine, and say so plainly.

never include a row in an error message

title: Most edge functions do not require a JWT, and that is a design rather than a gap
content:
A large majority of the edge functions in this estate are deployed with JWT verification switched off, and only a small minority require one at the platform level. Reading that as a security hole is the wrong first conclusion, and reading it as fine is the wrong second one. Both mistakes are common enough to justify a record.

Why it is a design. Functions that must be reachable by a machine caller carrying a shared secret, by a webhook signed by a third party, or by a browser presenting a token the function itself wants to inspect, all need to receive the request before deciding. Platform-level verification would reject the request before the function could apply the check that actually belongs to it. So those functions self-verify: they read the bearer and resolve it to a user themselves, or they verify a provider signature, or they compare a shared secret.

Why it is not automatically fine. The property that matters is not whether the platform verified a JWT, it is whether EVERY path through the function performs a check appropriate to its caller before doing anything privileged. A function with verification off and no self-check is open to the internet. A function with verification off that self-checks on the main path but not on an early branch is open on that branch.

So the audit question is per function and per path, never a count. When reviewing one, find the first line that does something privileged -- a write, a read of another party's data, a spend, a message -- and confirm that no path reaches it without an identity decision.

The estate pins the verification setting in the repository and checks it for drift, so an unexplained change to that setting on a deployed function is itself a signal worth investigating regardless of whether the function is otherwise sound.

structured_data.observation: most functions deploy with JWT verification off; only a small minority require one at the platform level

title: Payment has two facts and the second one is the fragile one
content:
Payment runs through Stripe hosted Checkout: the customer is redirected to a page Stripe serves, card details never touch this estate, and no card number is stored -- only Stripe's own references. That is what keeps the compliance scope minimal, and the security corpus covers the scope question properly.

For a monitoring seat, the operational shape is what matters, and it is the two-facts pattern in its purest form. Fact one: the customer paid, which is true at Stripe. Fact two: we know they paid, which becomes true here only when a webhook arrives, its signature is verified, and a row is written. Those are different events with different failure modes, and almost every payment incident is a failure of the second while the first succeeded.

What that means practically. A customer insisting they paid and a database saying they did not are frequently BOTH correct, and the fix is never to take their word and never to dismiss them -- it is to reconcile against Stripe, which is the authority for fact one. The webhook is a notification about the truth, not the truth.

The things that break fact two: a signature verification failure, which is correct behaviour refusing a request and must never be relaxed to make an error go away; a handler error after verification, which is the dangerous one because the event was accepted and then lost; a duplicate delivery handled non-idempotently; and an endpoint that was unreachable during a deploy, where Stripe retries but the retry window is finite.

The monitor to want is a reconciliation rather than an error rate: periodically compare completed payments at Stripe against recorded payments here for the same window, and alert on the DIFFERENCE. An error-rate monitor on the webhook cannot see the events that never arrived, which is the failure it most needs to catch.

title: Email and messaging: acceptance is not delivery, and the outbox is where the truth is
content:
Outbound email goes through Resend and outbound WhatsApp and SMS through Twilio. Both providers accept a message and then deliver it asynchronously, which means there are at least three distinct states and confusing them is the single most common messaging misdiagnosis: we tried to send, the provider accepted, and the recipient received. Only the third is delivery, and this estate can observe the first two directly and the third only through provider feedback.

The queued-notification path is driven from the scheduler tick rather than from the database, so the flush depends on the heartbeat running. A backlog on the messaging channel therefore has two quite different causes -- the provider is refusing, or the flusher is not being called -- and they need different responses. Distinguish them by looking at whether ANY message left in the window: none at all points at the flusher, some but not enough points at the provider or at a per-run batch limit.

The batch limits matter and are easy to misread. The scheduler drives sending in bounded batches, so a backlog larger than the batch size drains over several ticks by design. A backlog that is merely large is not necessarily an incident; a backlog whose OLDEST item is getting older tick after tick is, because that means arrival is outstripping drain or the drain has stopped.

And the status-column lens applies here with full force: a row marked sent was marked by the code that called the provider. Whether the provider accepted, and whether the recipient received, are separate facts held elsewhere. When somebody asks whether a customer was contacted, the honest answer comes from the outbox and the provider, not from the subject record.

Suppression is a real and correct reason for non-delivery. Check it early, because it looks exactly like a bug and is not one.

structured_data.observable_here: the first two directly; the third only through provider feedback
structured_data.flush_dependency: the queued path is driven by the scheduler tick, so it depends on the heartbeat running
structured_data.backlog_triage: none left in the window points at the flusher; some but not enough points at the provider or a batch limit
structured_data.batch_limits: sending is bounded per run, so a large backlog drains over several ticks by design
structured_data.real_alert: the age of the OLDEST unsent item rising tick after tick, not the size of the backlog
structured_data.suppression: a correct reason for non-delivery that looks exactly like a bug -- check it early

title: There are two agent seats and no departments, and work that fits neither is a finding
content:
On 7 September 2026 the founder removed the organisational structure entirely. In his words the chart was to be removed rather than archived, there are to be no departments, and no task exists unless he confirmed it. What remains is two seats: a chief executive seat and a customer support seat, which is the messaging agent. A large number of components are deliberately unowned and stay that way until he sets a new structure.

Why an IT seat needs this in its knowledge rather than treating it as governance trivia. First, it bounds what an alert may DO. Routing a finding to a department is not available; there is no department to route to. Opening a task nobody confirmed is not available either. Second, it explains a class of thing you will find while investigating: routines, tables and checks that reference roles, departments, workflows and handoffs which no longer exist. Those are residue of the removal, not corruption, and encountering one is not by itself an incident.

Third, and most practically, it tells you what to do when work does not fit. If a finding belongs to neither seat, the correct action is to state that plainly as the finding rather than to invent an owner for it. Inventing a third seat, writing a department into anything, or rebuilding a workflow registry are all specifically excluded.

Two guards survived the removal deliberately and must not be treated as residue: the protection against wholesale table truncation, on the grounds that wiping a whole table is never a legitimate operation and always a mistake, and the check that the anonymous role cannot execute a privileged routine. The first is correctness, the second is security, and neither is structure.

When the new structure exists, checks get written against THAT. A check edited until it passes against an empty schema asserts nothing while still looking like a guard.

title: Most of the business logic is in the database, and what that changes about diagnosis
content:
This is not an application with a database behind it. It is a database with functions in front of it. The great majority of the business rules -- eligibility, pricing, state transitions, guards, routing, reporting -- are Postgres routines, and the edge functions are largely transport: authenticate, marshal, call a routine, return the result.

Five things follow, and each changes where you look first.

A bug is more often in a routine than in a function. When an endpoint returns a wrong answer at a successful status, read the routine it calls before reading the handler, because the handler usually just forwarded what it got.

A change can be live without a deploy. Applying SQL replaces a routine immediately, with no pipeline and no build. So a behaviour that changed with no corresponding function deploy is not a mystery; check when the routine was last replaced.

Guards run inside the transaction, which is why they are effective and also why they surface as errors rather than as validation messages. A constraint or a trigger refusing a write appears to the caller as a database error, and a handler that catches broadly will convert a correct refusal into a silent no-op.

Trigger order is by name, not by definition order or by intent. Before-triggers fire alphabetically, which is why naming prefixes exist. A trigger renamed without regard to this changes behaviour without changing a line of logic.

And null semantics bite differently in a rule engine than in application code. The least and greatest functions IGNORE nulls, so a bound computed with a null argument silently returns the other argument rather than null -- a cap that quietly stops capping. Any comparison written on the assumption that null propagates needs checking against what Postgres actually does.

title: The company is pre-launch, which changes what an empty table means and what it does not
content:
Customers, inquiries, quotes and transactions sit at zero. Suppliers are an invited pool that has not converted. This is the expected state of a business that has not opened, and it must not be reported as a defect, a blocker or a caveat -- the founder has said so repeatedly and it wastes his time.

What it DOES change for a monitoring seat is what a number means, and getting this wrong in either direction is costly.

An empty table is not evidence of a fault. Neither is a rate of zero, a queue of zero, or a guard that has never fired. Nothing has been asked of these paths.

But equally, an empty table is not evidence that anything WORKS. The paths have not been exercised, so their behaviour is unknown rather than good. A monitor that has never had a non-zero input has not been validated; a guard that has never been reached has not been shown to fire; an integration that has never carried traffic is not connected.

So the correct posture is to build against the SHAPE of the data rather than its presence, and to validate by driving synthetic cases through the real entry points rather than by waiting for reality. That is the standing instruction: build the pipe now, the water comes later, and prove the pipe with water you poured yourself.

The boundary on how that is done is absolute. Validation happens in a sandbox with synthetic identities following the demo convention -- a marked name and an invalid-by-construction email domain -- and inside aborted transactions where the write can be counted and then rolled back. Never with a real customer, a real supplier, a real inquiry or real money. A live pilot to see if it works IS launching, and it is not on the table.

And because probes run against production routines, a probe that touches an alerting path can page the founder. Run fixtures through whatever wrapper suppresses that, and check before you run, not after.
